title: Taapsee Pannu Says Bollywood Still Won't Invest in Women-Led Action Films
excerpt: Ahead of her Netflix action-drama Gandhari, the actress calls out Bollywood's persistent budget gap between male-led and female-led films, saying expensive technology needed for high-end action remains out of reach for women-fronted projects.
body:
• Taapsee Pannu says women-led action films in Bollywood continue to receive significantly smaller budgets than male-led counterparts, limiting the scale of action sequences possible
  • The actress returns to the action genre with Netflix's Gandhari, releasing September 3, directed by Devashish Makhija and written by Kanika Dhillon
  • Pannu has deliberately avoided typecasting by seeking unpredictable roles, crediting films like Soorma, Mission Mangal, and Dunki for helping her break out of intense character types
  • She also highlighted ageism in the industry, describing being told she was too old for romantic comedies after turning 30

Taapsee Pannu has never been one to shy away from Bollywood's uncomfortable truths. Ahead of her return to the action genre with Netflix's Gandhari, the 39-year-old actress is calling out what she sees as the industry's persistent reluctance to invest in women-led films at the same scale as their male-led counterparts.

The Budget Gap That Won't Close

"We have come quite far with men doing action because exponentially a much higher number of films have been made, where men have done action, so the budgets of those films are way ahead," Pannu told Cinema Express in an interview this week.

The issue, she says, is not a lack of talent or audience appetite but a structural underinvestment that limits what female-led projects can achieve on screen.

"Unfortunately, with women doing action, we haven't reached those numbers in terms of investment. Some things require technology, and technology is extremely expensive."

— Taapsee Pannu

It is an observation Pannu has returned to throughout her career. In previous interviews, she has pointed out that the entire budget of a female-led A-list film in Bollywood often equals a single male actor's fee — a disparity she has called "insane." Audiences, she has argued, are part of the equation: pre-booking for male protagonist films while waiting for reviews before watching a female-led one.

A Decade Later, Back to Action

Gandhari, releasing September 3 on Netflix, marks Pannu's return to the action genre nearly a decade after her breakout role as a spy in Neeraj Pandey's Baby (2015) and its 2017 spin-off Naam Shabana. Directed by Devashish Makhija and written by Kanika Dhillon, the film casts Pannu as a mother who takes matters into her own hands after her daughter is kidnapped.

"It's a story about the lengths a parent will go to for their child," she said, framing Gandhari as a character-driven narrative rather than a conventional crime drama. The cast includes Ishwak Singh, Chhaya Kadam, Swastika Mukherjee, Mita Vashisht, and Jatin Sarna.

Breaking the Mold

Pannu also spoke about her deliberate effort to avoid typecasting. After being pushed toward intense, dramatic roles early in her Hindi film career — largely because conventional mainstream parts were not available to her — she has sought out characters that audiences would not necessarily expect.

"From the beginning of my career, I had no options in regular mainstream cliched roles, which are actually money-spinners for actresses. I didn't get those kinds of roles; hence I took the other type of roles, and to my luck, those films and roles later became mainstream," she told Cinema Express.

She credited films like Soorma, Mission Mangal, and Dunki with Shah Rukh Khan for providing a needed reprieve from the psychological toll of portraying heavy characters back-to-back. Her role as an influencer in Khel Khel Mein, she said, was a deliberate experiment in unpredictability.

Ageism Compounds the Problem

The investment gap is compounded by ageism. In an interview earlier this year, Pannu described being told she was "not young enough" for romantic comedies after turning 30, even for roles where the character's age was irrelevant.

"By the time you make a mark, you've crossed 30. Then they say you're not young enough to be featured in a rom-com. It doesn't really happen the same way with men," she told Times Entertainment, as reported by Filmfare.

She noted that the bias operated differently in South Indian cinema, where working opposite a senior actor could tag an actress as "too senior" for younger male leads. "You dare say that about Shah Rukh Khan," she said. "An actress's life changes after working with Shah Rukh Khan. But that taboo was there for me when I worked in the South."

Still, Pannu sees reasons for optimism. Streaming platforms have expanded career longevity for actresses, and pan-India hits have shown that audiences will turn out for women-led stories. Gandhari, she hopes, will add to that evidence — even if the budget behind it reflects an industry still catching up to its own rhetoric about equality.
